name: product-planning
description: Two-speaker product planning meeting. Synthetic, so it has no overlap, no crosstalk and no room noise — it exercises meeting vocabulary (names, dates, numbers, jargon, action items) and validates the harness, but it is easier than any real recording. Treat WER from this fixture as a floor, never as the product number.
lines: Alright, let's get started. Marcus, can you walk us through where the capture pipeline landed this week?
Sure. The big change is that partial results now carry an utterance identifier, so we can tell two overlapping speakers apart instead of collapsing them into one caption line.
That was the bug where the system channel would overwrite itself, right?
Exactly that. If two people on the call talked at the same time, the second partial replaced the first, and whichever arrived last won. It looked like the transcript was losing words at random.
How confident are we that it's actually fixed?

Reasonably. I added a keyed map so each live utterance has its own slot. The remaining risk is ordering — a late partial can still arrive after a newer one, and right now we take the last message rather than the highest sequence number.
No, maybe half a day. The providers already send a sequence field, we just throw it away at the adapter boundary.
Let's close it. I don't want to ship something that's ninety percent right on the exact thing we said we fixed.
Good. What about the rebuild cost? You flagged something about the transcript being reassembled on every segment.

Yeah, that one's uglier. Every time a segment finalizes we rebuild the entire transcript string and write it into the store. On a five minute meeting that's fine. On a ninety minute meeting the last segment is rebuilding something like forty thousand characters, sixty times a minute.
Which is presumably why the panel gets janky about an hour in.
That's my read. Nobody tests a ninety minute meeting, so it never showed up in review.
Derive it lazily. The store keeps the segment list, and anything that wants a flat string asks for one at the moment it needs it. Nothing in the hot path touches the whole transcript.
Any risk to the write-up flow? That reads the flat transcript.
It reads it once, at the end. That's exactly the case lazy derivation handles well.
Okay. Put that in the same change set.
Will do. Second thing — I want to talk about model selection, because I think we've been guessing.

We've been saying the baseline machine is an eighth or ninth generation i5 with eight gigabytes of memory, and that a six hundred million parameter streaming model will hold real time on it. I can't find where that was ever measured.
I don't think it was. I think it came out of a vendor benchmark.

Right, and vendor benchmarks are throughput numbers on a server part. Throughput isn't the question. The question is whether captions stay next to the speaker for an hour on a laptop that's also running a browser and a video call.
Those are different questions how, exactly?

Throughput says how fast the decoder chews through a file when you hand it everything at once. Latency says how long after somebody speaks the words appear. A model can be twice real time on throughput and still feel two seconds behind, because the chunk size and the flush behaviour dominate.
So what would you actually measure?

Four things. Real time factor, so we know there's headroom at all. Peak resident memory, because eight gigabytes is the constraint that bites first. Caption latency under a one-times feed. And word error rate against a corrected reference, so we're not trading accuracy for speed without noticing.

A day, if we have a machine. The harness is the easy part. The hard part is getting ten minutes of representative audio — two speakers, some overlap, some background noise. Clean read speech will flatter every model equally and tell us nothing.

That's the thing I need from you. It has to be a physical low-end laptop, not a throttled virtual machine. Memory bandwidth and thermal behaviour are exactly what's in question, and a virtual machine misrepresents both.
Let me check what's in the hardware cupboard. I think there's a Dell from about twenty nineteen.
That would be close enough if it has eight gigabytes.
I'll confirm by Thursday. What happens if the answer is no, it doesn't hold real time?

Then the tier matrix changes before anyone builds against it, which is the whole point of measuring first. We'd probably drop the baseline tier to a smaller model and accept visibly worse captions on old hardware, or we stage the download so people get something usable immediately and the better model arrives in the background.
Staged is nicer and more work.
Staged is nicer and more work, yes.
Let's not decide that until we have numbers. Anything else?

One more. The indexing path fails silently. When a note gets embedded, the call is fire and forget with an empty catch. If the vector database is down, or the embedding worker crashed, the note just never becomes searchable and nothing tells anyone.
They wouldn't. They'd search for a meeting they remember, get nothing, and conclude the search is bad.
Much worse. And the odd part is that deletes already have durable retry — there's a pending purge table. Writes have nothing. So we're careful about removing a vector and careless about creating one.
What's the shape of the fix?

Add a column that records when a chunk was embedded. If it's null, it's queued. A background pass picks up anything null and retries with backoff. It also makes progress reportable, because how much is left becomes a single count query.
I like that. It's the same table, no new machinery.

Okay. Let me read back what I've got. You're closing the sequence ordering gap and the transcript rebuild in one change set. You're building the measurement harness. I'm confirming a baseline laptop by Thursday. And the indexing queue is scoped but not scheduled.
That's right. I'd put the indexing queue after the measurement work, because if the model tiering changes we might be re-embedding everything anyway.
Fair. Let's revisit it next Tuesday once we know.
One last thing, and this is more of a heads up than a decision. Legal wants the privacy language nailed down before we talk about the hosted tier publicly.
Because of the relay. If somebody subscribes, their transcript goes to our server and then on to a model provider. That's two hops, and we've been describing the product as local first.
Both things can be true, but only if we say which one is happening at the moment it happens.
That's exactly the position. Local stays local, hosted is clearly marked, and we publish what the relay retains, which should be nothing.
Zero retention is the only version I'd be comfortable defending.
Same. I'll get that written down. Alright, that's time. Thanks everyone.
